ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: The at-ease person of the Way appears chiefly in the compound “one at ease, with learning ended and nothing contrived,” which the records treat as a named condition rather than mere leisure.
EvidenceBody: Literally, "an idle or at-ease person of the Way" . Chan usage bends ordinary idleness into a named epithet, most often in the full line "an at-ease person of the Way who has ended study and does nothing contrived" . Huangbo explains that people of old heard one statement and thereby "ended study" , and so received this name; he contrasts them with people seeking much knowledge and many explanations. Tianru explicitly lists "the great sea of extinction" , "the ground of actual principle" , and this full epithet as different names for "great rest" . The Mirror Record distinguishes accumulating study, ending study, and then passing beyond both, saying that only on reaching the end of study does one first draw near the Way. Other records deploy the shortened term in verse: the whole world is full of people seeking buddha, but an at-ease person of the Way is hard to find . The epithet therefore names a Chan roster type through explicit ending-study and great-rest definitions, not a generic loafer.
